title: Accuracy, Sentence Variety & Proofreading
description: W5 error triage and W3 sentence control under exam timing — which errors cost most, how to vary sentences deliberately, and a five-minute proofreading protocol.

notes.heading: Where Accuracy Is Marked (and Where It Is Not)
notes.body: W5 — accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar — is named in Paper 2: Question 1(b) shares 25 writing marks with W1–W4, and Section B Composition carries 40 writing marks including W5. Paper 1's writing marks name W1–W3 (Question 2(a)) and W1–W4 (Question 4) — W5 is absent from the paper, so accuracy is not separately rewarded there — but writing an examiner cannot decode still damages everything else. The level descriptors tell you how W5 is judged: top-band scripts are accurate throughout, while the bottom bands describe errors so frequent they impede communication. Note the direction of travel: a single misspelling does not sink you, but errors that break meaning do. That is why accuracy under time pressure is a triage problem, not a neatness problem — and why ambitious vocabulary you cannot spell is a trap, since it threatens W5 while chasing W3.

notes.heading: Error Triage: What Costs Most
notes.body: Not all errors are equal under W5. The descriptors penalise errors that impede communication, so the hierarchy is: (1) Sentence-boundary faults — comma splices, fused sentences and accidental fragments make the examiner re-read to find where one idea ends; these are the most damaging per occurrence. (2) Verb control — tense drift and subject-verb disagreement confuse when something happens and who is doing it; both are common in narratives written at speed. (3) Surface slips — a homophone swap ('their' for 'there'), a missing comma, a misspelled common word: noticed, but they rarely break meaning. When the clock is short, fix in that order: one repaired comma splice is worth more than three corrected spellings. The trap is spending your last five minutes hunting spelling mistakes while two fused sentences sit in paragraph one. KS3 Grammar & Punctuation and Punctuation Mastery teach the rules themselves; this topic is about deploying them when it counts.

illustration.alt: A three-tier error-triage pyramid — sentence boundaries at the top, verb control in the middle, surface slips at the base — beside a four-pass proofreading protocol.
illustration.caption: Triage under time pressure: fix sentence boundaries first, then verbs, then surface slips — and proofread in four single-job passes.

notes.heading: Sentence Boundaries Under Pressure
notes.body: The comma splice — joining two complete sentences with only a comma ('The whistle blew, the crowd surged forward') — is the most common serious fault in timed writing. Its cousin is the fused sentence, with no punctuation at all ('The whistle blew the crowd surged forward'). Three fast repairs: split with a full stop ('The whistle blew. The crowd surged forward.'); join with a semicolon when the ideas are tightly linked; or add a conjunction ('The whistle blew, and the crowd surged forward.'). Fragments are the mirror problem: 'Running as fast as she could.' has no main verb and is an accident, while 'Silence.' after a paragraph of noise is a deliberate device. The test is intention and rarity — an accidental fragment breaks W5, while a rare, obviously deliberate one earns W3 credit for control. In the exam, interrogate every comma with one question: could each side of it stand alone? If both sides can, the comma is wrong.

notes.heading: Sentence Variety: A Marked Skill, Not a Decoration
notes.body: W3 explicitly rewards a range of sentence structures used for effect, so variety is marks, not decoration. Build it deliberately. Mix the three structures: simple ('The door slammed.') for impact; compound ('The door slammed, and the lights went out.') for balance; complex ('When the door slammed, the lights went out.') to show the relationship between ideas. Vary your openings: start with an adverb ('Slowly, the fog lifted.'), a connective ('Despite the warning, they pressed on.'), or a subordinate clause ('Although exhausted, she kept climbing.') instead of beginning every sentence with 'I', 'The' or 'Then'. Use the one-sentence paragraph or the two-word sentence for a deliberate jolt — sparingly, because the device works through rarity. The failure mode to avoid is the opposite of monotony: sentences so long and tangled that the grammar collapses inside them. Controlled variety beats ambitious chaos every time.

notes.heading: Vocabulary: Precision Over Decoration
notes.body: W3 rewards a range of vocabulary appropriate to context — the operative word is appropriate. Precise means specific and exact: 'the soup was watery and over-salted' says more than 'the food was nice', and more than 'the repast was unpalatable', which is thesaurus abuse — a fancy word deployed for impressiveness rather than meaning. Three rules for exam writing. One: choose the word whose meaning you are certain of; a misused ambitious word costs more than a plain correct one. Two: only use words you can spell — a misspelled ambitious word damages W5 while trying to impress W3. Three: match vocabulary to register (see Audience, Register & Form): 'conflagration' might suit a report, but not a journal entry about a barbecue. Upgrade weak words where it counts: verbs and nouns first ('trudged', 'gale'), adjectives and adverbs sparingly.

notes.heading: The Five-Minute Proofreading Protocol
notes.body: Proofreading a 350–450 word composition in one read catches almost nothing, because your brain reads what you meant to write. Work in passes, one job per pass. Pass 1 (one minute): read for sense, hearing the words in your head — any sentence you have to re-read gets simplified or split. Pass 2 (ninety seconds): sentence boundaries only — hunt comma splices, fused sentences and accidental fragments. Pass 3 (ninety seconds): verbs — check tense consistency (narratives drift between past and present) and subject-verb agreement, especially when words intervene ('the box of old photographs were…'). Pass 4 (one minute): the spelling of ambitious words and the classic confusables — their/there/they're, its/it's, your/you're. Corrections should be neat: a single line through the error, the correction written above. Do not rewrite whole sentences in the final minutes; a clean, corrected script reads better than a frantic palimpsest.

notes.heading: Confusable Traps and the Practice Route
notes.body: Certain confusions recur at this level because speech hides them: 'should of' for 'should have' (the spoken 'should've' deceives the ear); their/there/they're; your/you're; its/it's (the apostrophe belongs to the contraction 'it is' — the possessive 'its' has none, just like 'his'); whose/who's; affect/effect (affect is usually the verb, effect the noun); then/than; practice/practise (in British English, practice is the noun and practise the verb). KS3 Spelling Strategies covers memory tricks for these — revise them there. In the exam, your Pass 4 should sweep specifically for whichever confusions you personally make: keep a private hit-list from your marked work. And practise under real conditions: the course's free-response practice sets are marked by AI that reports your error patterns, which is how a hit-list gets built in the first place. Accuracy improves through marked practice, not through re-reading rules.

flashcards.definition: Two complete sentences joined by only a comma; a serious sentence-boundary fault under W5.
flashcards.example: 'The whistle blew, the crowd surged forward' — fix with a full stop, semicolon or conjunction.

flashcards.definition: Two complete sentences run together with no punctuation at all; also called a run-on.
flashcards.example: 'The match was cancelled it was raining' needs a boundary: '…cancelled because it was raining.'

flashcards.definition: Words punctuated as a sentence but lacking a main verb or subject; an error unless clearly deliberate.
flashcards.example: 'Running as fast as she could.' is an accident; 'Silence.' can be a device.

flashcards.definition: Slipping between past and present tense within a piece; confusing for the reader, costly under W5.
flashcards.example: 'I walked into the hall and the lights go out' drifts from past to present.

flashcards.definition: Matching the verb to its true subject, ignoring words that intervene.
flashcards.example: 'The box of old photographs was on the desk' — the subject is 'box', not 'photographs'.

flashcards.definition: Words that sound alike but differ in meaning or spelling, e.g. their/there/they're.
flashcards.example: 'The team celebrated their victory' — possessive 'their', never 'there'.

flashcards.definition: A short verbless sentence used intentionally for effect; effective only when rare.
flashcards.example: 'Silence. Then the floorboard creaked above her.' — the pause is the point.

flashcards.definition: Deliberately mixing simple, compound and complex sentences with varied openings; rewarded by W3.
flashcards.example: 'Slowly, the fog lifted. What it revealed made them stop.'

flashcards.definition: Choosing an impressive word over a precise one; a misused ambitious word costs more than a plain one.
flashcards.example: 'She perambulated home' is decoration; 'she trudged home' is precision.

flashcards.definition: Never 'should of': the spoken 'should've' deceives the ear into writing 'of'.
flashcards.example: 'I should have studied' — expand the contraction to check.

flashcards.definition: 'It's' means 'it is'; the possessive 'its' has no apostrophe, just like 'his'.
flashcards.example: 'It's raining' but 'the dog wagged its tail'.

flashcards.definition: 'Affect' is usually the verb (to influence); 'effect' is usually the noun (the result).
flashcards.example: 'The storm affected the match' — 'the effect was a cancellation'.

choices: A varied range of sentence structures
Accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar
Language matched to audience and purpose
Understanding of a writer's techniques
questions.explanation: W5 is the accuracy objective: spelling, punctuation and grammar. Sentence range is W3, audience-and-purpose fit is W4, and analysing a writer's techniques is the reading objective R4. Knowing which objective pays for which skill tells you where your exam effort goes — W5 is named in Paper 2's writing marks.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a comma splice?
choices: The whistle blew, and the crowd surged forward.
The whistle blew; the crowd surged forward.
The whistle blew. The crowd surged forward.
The whistle blew, the crowd surged forward.
questions.explanation: The last option joins two complete sentences with nothing but a comma — the definition of a comma splice. The first adds the conjunction 'and', the second uses a semicolon, and the third splits with a full stop: all three are the standard repairs for exactly this fault.

questions.stem: What is the best repair for the fused sentence 'The match was cancelled it was raining.'?
choices: The match was cancelled because it was raining.
The match was cancelled, it was raining.
The match was cancelled it was raining, unfortunately.
The match was, cancelled, it was raining.
questions.explanation: Adding the conjunction 'because' both fixes the boundary and explains the relationship between the two ideas. Adding a comma alone creates a comma splice; adding 'unfortunately' changes nothing about the missing boundary; scattering commas makes it worse. A full stop or semicolon would also have fixed it.

questions.stem: Which paragraph keeps its tense under control?
choices: I walked into the hall and the lights go out. Everyone is screaming and I ran for the door.
I walk into the hall. The lights went out. Everyone was screaming as I run for the door.
I walked into the hall and the lights went out. Everyone was screaming as I ran for the door.
I walked into the hall and the lights will go out. Everyone was screaming as I ran for the door.
questions.explanation: The third option stays in the past tense throughout: walked, went, was screaming, ran. The others drift — starting past and flipping to present ('go', 'is'), mixing present with past ('walk' then 'went'), or jumping to the future ('will go'). Tense drift like this is exactly the verb-control error the second tier of W5 triage targets.

questions.stem: 'I should of studied more.' What is the error?
choices: There is no error; this is standard written English.
'Of' should be 'have' — speech disguises 'should've' as 'should of'.
'Should' should be 'would' in formal writing.
The sentence needs a comma after 'I'.
questions.explanation: The contraction 'should've' sounds like 'should of', which is why the error is so common — but the verb is 'should have', and 'should of' is never correct in standard English. Swapping in 'would' changes the meaning, and no comma is needed after the subject.

questions.stem: Which fragment is most likely to be read as deliberate and effective?
choices: Running as fast as she could.
Because the storm was getting worse.
Which was the last thing anyone expected.
Silence. Then the floorboard creaked above her.
questions.explanation: 'Silence.' earns its keep: it is a deliberate, one-word pause for effect, immediately followed by controlled, complete sentences. The other three are accidental fragments — a participle phrase and two dependent clauses punctuated as sentences — which examiners read as boundary errors under W5, not as style.

questions.stem: With two minutes left in the exam, which fix should take priority?
choices: Splitting a fused sentence in the second paragraph
Changing a slightly repetitive but correct word choice
Adding a comma after an opening phrase
Correcting the capital letter on a proper noun
questions.explanation: Sentence-boundary faults sit at the top of the triage pyramid because they impede communication, which is what the W5 descriptors penalise most heavily. Repetitive diction, an optional comma and a single capital slip are all surface-level issues: noticed, but far cheaper than a sentence the examiner has to untangle.

questions.stem: A paragraph reads: 'I entered the room. I saw the crowd. I felt my knees shake.' Which revision best improves it for W3?
choices: I entered the room. I saw the crowd. I felt my knees shake. I was nervous.
I very nervously entered the very crowded room and very much felt my knees shake.
As I entered the room, the sight of the crowd made my knees shake.
I entered the room, and I saw the crowd, and I felt my knees shake, and I was terrified.
questions.explanation: The complex-sentence revision subordinates one idea to another and varies the opening, which is what W3 rewards. The first option just adds a fourth simple sentence; the second swaps in empty intensifiers rather than restructuring; the third chains 'and' into a run of equal clauses — variety in name only.

questions.stem: 'The team celebrated ___ victory.' Which word completes the sentence?
choices: there
their
they're
theirs
questions.explanation: The sentence needs the possessive 'their' — the victory belongs to the team. 'There' is a place, 'they're' means 'they are' (which makes no sense before a noun), and 'theirs' stands alone rather than sitting before a noun. Sound-alike confusions like this are why the final proofreading pass exists.

questions.stem: Which replacement word is the most precise, rather than merely fancier?
choices: 'The meal was gastronomical' instead of 'The meal was good'
'She perambulated home' instead of 'She walked home'
'The film was diabolical' chosen over 'terrible' purely to impress
'He trudged home' instead of 'He walked home tiredly'
questions.explanation: 'Trudged' earns its place: it is an exact word that fuses walking and exhaustion into one precise verb. The others decorate instead of specifying — 'gastronomical' is misused (it describes the art of food, not its quality), 'perambulated' is showy where 'walked' is natural, and swapping 'terrible' for 'diabolical' adds no meaning. W3 rewards precision appropriate to context, not syllable count.

questions.stem: Why does the proofreading protocol check sentence boundaries before spelling?
choices: Boundary faults impede communication, which the mark scheme penalises far more than surface slips
Spelling errors cannot be fixed once the sentence boundaries are set
Examiners only read the first pass of corrections
Boundary checks are quicker, so they should always go first in any task
questions.explanation: The triage logic comes straight from the level descriptors: errors that break meaning — splices, fused sentences, accidental fragments — drag a script towards the band where errors impede communication, while a spelling slip rarely does. Spelling is fixable at any point (the second option is false), examiners read the final script rather than the passes, and speed is a convenience, not the principle.

questions.stem: 'The box of old photographs ___ on the desk.' Which verb form is correct?
choices: were
are
was
have been
questions.explanation: The subject is 'the box' (singular), not 'photographs' — the interrupting phrase 'of old photographs' is the classic agreement trap, so the verb is 'was'. 'Were', 'are' and 'have been' all agree with the nearer plural noun instead of the true subject. In your verb pass, find the subject first, ignoring everything after 'of'.

choices: The dog wagged it's tail.
Its raining again, so the match is off.
The committee has made it's decision.
It's the last train, so we should leave now.
questions.explanation: 'It's' with the apostrophe means 'it is' — exactly right here. The possessive 'its' never takes an apostrophe, so 'it's tail' and 'it's decision' are wrong, and 'Its raining' drops the apostrophe the contraction needs. The quick test: expand to 'it is' and see whether the sentence still makes sense.

questions.stem: 'He opened the door. He saw the crowd. He froze.' Which single edit most improves W3 credit?
choices: Opening the door, he saw the crowd — and froze.
He opened the door, he saw the crowd, he froze.
He opened the door and he saw the crowd and he froze.
Suddenly, he opened the door. Suddenly, he saw the crowd. Suddenly, he froze.
questions.explanation: The first revision varies the sentence opening with a participle phrase, subordinates the actions into one controlled complex sentence and uses the dash for a deliberate pause — a range of structures used for effect, which is W3's wording. The comma version is a double comma splice, the 'and' chain is monotony in a longer wrapper, and repeating 'Suddenly' three times trades one pattern for another.

questions.stem: Why should you only use ambitious vocabulary you can also spell?
choices: Because examiners are not allowed to credit any word with a spelling error
Because plain vocabulary is always safer and ambition is never rewarded
Because a misspelled ambitious word threatens W5 accuracy while trying to earn W3 range
Because dictionaries are banned, so ambition is impossible to check
questions.explanation: The two objectives collide here: W3 rewards a range of appropriate vocabulary, but W5 penalises inaccurate spelling, so an ambitious word you cannot spell risks both at once. Words with errors can still carry meaning (the first option overstates it), and W3 explicitly wants range, so plain-only writing is not the answer (the second). The fourth is a non-sequitur — dictionaries are banned, but careful word choice is still possible.
